title: Simhika, the shadow-catcher
hook: a shadow-catcher drags Hanuman down, and the reason families read this book when life gets hard
carry: in hard times, families read the sundara kanda

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Hanuman the size of a thumb, and Surasa's rule and his promise, both kept at once.

Hanuman is flying fast, Surasa's blessing behind him, the sea open ahead. He has met a mountain and a serpent mother out here, and both of them he could see. Then, all at once, his speed fails. He's being held back, Valmiki says, like a great ship against a contrary wind. No storm, no wall, no monster. Every stretch of air takes more effort than the last, and when he looks around, there's nothing there.
screen: `HIS SPEED FAILS.` → `LIKE A SHIP AGAINST THE WIND.` → `NOTHING THERE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman looks up, down, left, right. Then he looks below, at the water, and sees her. A huge creature has risen from the sea: Simhika, a rakshasi, a demoness who catches flying things by their shadows. She has seized Hanuman's shadow where it falls on the waves, and through it she is dragging him down. And Hanuman knows what she is. Valmiki says he remembers: this is the shadow-catching creature Sugriva, the monkey king, warned the searchers about before they set out. So the slowing wasn't weakness. It had a name, and now he can face it. Simhika is not like Surasa. Surasa was a test sent by the gods. Simhika simply wants to eat whatever flies over her water. She opens her mouth wide, and Hanuman gets ready. Here's why this part of the story lives in Hindu homes. This book of the Ramayana, the Sundara Kanda, is one obstacle after another: a mountain, a serpent mother, a shadow-catcher, each one met and passed by a messenger flying for Rama. So when life gets hard, a sickness, a lost job, a long wait, many Hindu families read the Sundara Kanda aloud, a portion each evening, in Valmiki's Sanskrit or in Tulsidas's Hindi retelling. It isn't read as a spell. They're walking beside Hanuman through his troubles while they walk through their own: looking down, naming what holds them, and flying on.
screen: `SHE HAS SEIZED HIS SHADOW.` · `SUGRIVA HAD WARNED THEM.` · `ONE OBSTACLE AFTER ANOTHER.` · then, large: `READ IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you, or someone at home, is carrying right now. If you pray, say Rama's name, or a line you know to Hanuman, slowly, a few times, the way families do on Sundara Kanda evenings. If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing quietly to yourself, as Hanuman named Simhika, and breathe with it. Once it has a name, it can be faced.
Simhika. The rakshasi in the southern sea who catches flying creatures by their shadows, and drags Hanuman down until he looks below and recognizes her.
Your line: in hard times, families read the Sundara Kanda. Tomorrow, Hanuman meets her open mouth. That's day six hundred ten.

Simhika.meaning: a demoness in the southern sea who catches creatures by their shadows

rakshasi.meaning: a female rakshasa, one of Ravana's kind

Sugriva.meaning: the monkey king, Rama's ally, who sent out the search

Surasa.meaning: the serpent mother who tested Hanuman and blessed him

Valmiki.meaning: the poet-sage traditionally credited with the Ramayana

Sundara Kanda.meaning: the beautiful book, the Ramayana's fifth, Hanuman's crossing and search
